scientific_question.whole_capitulum: Treat the capitulum as an integrated multivariate phenotype without assuming one syndrome or a fixed syndrome count.
scientific_question.scale_comparison: Compare trait organization within species versus among species before asking how environmental association geometry differs between those biological scales.

cohort.selection_rule: primary + candidate endpoint dimensions only; descriptive_only and validation_only excluded
cohort.hue_rule: corolla_hue_sin and corolla_hue_cos are one circular inferential unit

estimands.within_species: taxon-centred endpoint values with inverse taxon sample-size weights so each retained taxon contributes equal total weight
estimands.syndrome_assumption: none; no clustering or fixed syndrome count imposed

structure_results.interpretation: Trait organization is significantly partially shared across scales but not identical. Measurement-module integration is consistently stronger within species than among species, with a positive paired bootstrap difference at both minimum-support thresholds. Among-species phenotype space is also somewhat more concentrated in fewer leading dimensions, especially at min5.

environment_results.general_pattern: Among-species multivariate R2 exceeds within-species R2 for all six blocks at both support thresholds, but no block survives BH-FDR at either scale.
environment_results.cosine_bootstrap_note: All block-specific bootstrap 95% intervals include zero, so cross-scale environmental response-direction differences are descriptive rather than formally established in this analysis.
environment_results.interpretation: Environmental association geometry is weakly concordant or even oppositely oriented between biological scales, but current block-level omnibus evidence does not support a confirmatory claim that environment organizes the whole phenotype differently across scales.

claim_boundary: This analysis supports scale-dependent organization of the image-derived capitulum phenotype. It does not establish one genetic or functional syndrome, adaptation, causal environmental mechanisms, or a statistically confirmed cross-scale difference in environmental organization. The environmental scale-divergence result remains a descriptive hypothesis generated by the multivariate geometry.
